utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Case number IT-95-16-T. The Prosector versus Zoran Kupreskic, Mirjan Kupreskic, Vlatko Kupreskic, Drago Josipovic, Dragan Papic and Vladimir Santic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Good afternoon. We may continue. Mr. Radovic. Counsel Radovic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Good day. I don't have too many questions for you. Please tell me, in Zenica, what was the situation regarding receiving of information? Who did you get the information from about the events in Zenica in the region of Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I got a lot of of information from the people who were wounded, who were in the hospital in Cajdras, also from the villagers in my village who I lived with.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: What about the media?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The media, yes, through newspapers, television.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Did you buy newspapers at that time?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Which ones?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, which ones did we have? I can't recall right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But you know that already at that time --

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Just one moment. We had the Croatian press, Obitelj, something like that. Mr. Hammer was in charge.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: But this was not a newspaper that dealt with political issues. Did you have any kind of daily newspaper that reported about politics?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Did you read any newspapers at the time?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Mostly I got information from what people told me.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: So according to what people told you, from what you heard, did you hear what was happening in the region of Vitez from the 16th of April onwards?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: From the 16th of April, well, I didn't read about anything in the paper.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: So you didn't really hear anything. Did you hear anything from your patients, perhaps?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: From my patients? You mean from the 16th of of April?

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the events in Vitez from April 16th. Was the 16th of April significant to you in Zenica for any reason?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Did you watch television?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Did you have your own TV set at home?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Which TV stations could you receive at that time?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Only the ones that were in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: So this was Zetel?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, Zetel. And TVBH. This is Sarajevo television.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: So did you watch the news on those TV stations every day?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, not every day.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Did you see in any news programme, any TV programme? I assume that the news were on at 7.30 every evening just like they were in all the other areas of the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: So was there anything that related to Vitez?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, not about Vitez, but I remember now that on TV in Zenica the -- they showed on Zenica TV the foundation, the establishment of something in Zenica. And that is the first time I heard about Mr. Mario Kordic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Did you see any refugees from Vitez on television?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Did you see, maybe, any people who were recorded in the hospital in Zenica who were saying what they experienced in a village near Zenica called Ahmici, near Vitez called Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: You said that in the Croatian areas homes were usually torched after the Croats were expelled. Did I understand you right?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. The houses were torched after the Croats were expelled, but this happened on the 18th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Okay. So now we see that you don't know anything about the 16th. So now we're going to talk about the conduct of Muslim forces after they captured Croatian villages. What happened with the Croatian churches after the Muslims captured a Croatian village?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, they would shoot at the churches. The church in Cajdras is full of bullet holes. The priest and two nuns were abused in Cakrcici.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Any cross-examination by other counsel? Mrs. Slokovic-Glumac. Yes

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good day, Mrs. Tolic. You spoke about the situation in Zenica on the 15th of April, '93, after the murder of the escort and the capture of Zivko Totic. You also said there were problems in moving through the town.

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. I know this very well because that morning I was going to work, to the hospital in Cajdras. This is on the other side of the town from where I was living. I was living in Podbrezje. I went to work on foot and I could hear shooting earlier. I saw a car and I saw my late cousin there. I couldn't go further from that point. They turned me back. And then I reported to the headquarters of the HVO. They were consulting by phone with Cajdras, and they said, because my work colleagues already knew that it was difficult to move around the town, so they said that they would send an ambulance to get me, because I had to go there, get some medical equipment and come back to the headquarters, because I lived in Podbrezje, the command is 500 to 800 metres away from my house, less than a kilometre. I don't exactly know. Because they wanted -- because of the events that were taking place there, they wanted someone, a medical officer, to be in the command. And because I lived there, they asked me to come.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please slow down for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: So you got there with an ambulance?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: You said checkpoints were placed around the town.

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. I noticed this when I was leaving Podbrezje, when I was going from Trokuce to Cajdras there were police patrols and they had been increased compared to the previous days.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: The people who were at those checkpoints, were these members of the BiH Army or was this the police?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: It was the civilian police in dark uniforms, and there were also camouflage uniforms with black vests on top.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Do you remember whether they had --

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: They were completely armed. I don't know what you mean if they were completely armed. I know that they had pistols, they had batons in their hands. I'm not sure whether they had any guns. I didn't see that. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Did you notice at the entrance and exits to Zenica if there were any checkpoints there, any control points?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, I went to Cajdras and I must have encountered from the Travnik Street to Cajdras two of them. This was not usual. There were some in the centre of the city, close to the faculty of metallurgy in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: You also said in your testimony that in January of '93 you noticed men, people, from Busovaca, Muslims from Busovaca in Zenica, that they came by bus, if I understood you properly.

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No not by bus. Because my apartment was at the entrance to Zenica, it was four high-rise houses, so I lived in the first one of those buildings, close to the bridge, but I wasn't there all the time. I spent some time in my house in Podbrezje. But I would come and visit my apartment sometimes. So going from the apartment towards Podbrezje, this was the road going just below the house of corrections, and there's an army, a hold there. So I could see a truck standing by the road. I could also see an orange mini-van, but civilians were coming out of this truck, which was covered with tarpaulin. Women and children were coming out of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Do you recall whether this was before the conflict in Busovaca or after? You said that you were surprised when you saw them; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I was surprised, because I thought these were refugees from somewhere, and I stopped there because I always felt sorry for people who came from Gorazde, Potkozarje or wherever they would arrive from to Zenica. But there were a lot of refugees at that time. The department store, big buildings, were already occupied by refugees, so when I saw these women and children, I was -- I felt sorry for them and I asked them. So they said they were from Busovaca. And I was surprised, because I didn't know that anything was happening there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: All right. Also in your statement you said that you had heard that the HVO was being disarmed.

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Now we are talking about the 16th and the 17th of April of '93?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Who did you hear this from and how was this carried out?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I heard this after the 20th. On the 20th I left the house of correction of Zenica. I was at home. My friends were visiting me, who were living nearby. And then I heard this from them, because my brother-in-law, my husband's brother, was living close by. He wasn't a member of the HVO. He was a civilian in the house of correction. His wife, my sister-in-law, came as soon as I was released. And she heard, because she lives in Radakovo. I was also visited by other friends. She told me that on the 16th and the 17th they had already been disarmed there, on the right side of the bank of the River Bosna in the region of Cekrcici. That's where HOS was, but not all Croat members of HOS, but of the HVO. So I think in Drada Kovor, somewhere there, they had a kind of branch, the head coordinators in all regions. Because Croats were all over the place. So I heard that already on the 16th or the 17th they had been disarmed there, on the 17th, in the afternoon, that they had been surrounded -- that they had surrounded the HOS headquarters that was in the centre of the town, and I heard that some negotiations were being carried out for the members of the HOS to be released.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: So that's when the weapons were taken away from them?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. Some of them were also detained in the house of correction because when I arrived in my cell, there were already two women there who were members of HOS, they were Muslims, and I was in the cell together with them.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you, Counsel Slokovic-Glumac. I assume there is no other Defence counsel wishing to cross-examine this witness, so we move on to the Prosecution. Mr. Terrier?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I have only a few questions to put to the witness. I will be as concise as I can be.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Good morning, Madam. My name is Franck Terrier, I am a member of the Prosecution team, and it is my duty to put a number of questions to you. I hope it will be brief. Do you know the accused?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: You don't know any of them?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: None of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: According to a document that was given to us by the Defence, you actually reside in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Now I live in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Are you a nurse today as you were at the time of the events?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: In 1992 and 1993, were you a member of the HDZ?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Were you in any other way engaged in serving the Croatian cause at the time?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: '92 and '93; is that what you're asking me?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. When I left my job in the hospital, I moved to work in the crisis staff which was located in the Sestra Dietrich school. That's where the medical unit was being organised. This was in June '92.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: There is one thing I would like to understand. This duty you have just described to us, the aim of which was to help the injured, the ones who needed help, was also a political activity, wasn't it, because you were also defending the aim, that was the aim of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, I will say right away that I had nothing to do with politics.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Did you know Commander Totic?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Could you please be a little more specific about the unit he was commander of?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The military unit that he commanded in Zenica, I can only say about that that when he arrived, we expected a lot of him because we thought he was an expert, more expert than his predecessors at the crisis staff, that was Mr. Covic, his predecessor. I think he was very reliable. He was an honest man.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: There is something else I would like to know. What was the composition of the unit he commanded? How many men constituted that unit, how was it armed, what kind of weapons did it use?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I repeat again, I worked at the Sestre Dietrich school, and then when the commander came, Mr. Zivko Totic, we were transferred, and we worked in Cajdras, which means that I was not close to the headquarters or -- I can talk about the medical staff, how many were in our brigade, and it's possible that it numbered about 1.500 people. This is an approximate number.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: One thousand five hundred people. In Zenica, that is; is that what you mean? One thousand five hundred people in that unit?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: When he arrived at that time, there were no more than 1.500 people or so in the beginning. Then later, we had more Croats who joined us, the ones who were leaving the B and H army, and then at the end, just before the conflict around the 15th, some Croats from HOS also joined.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: At the beginning of April 1993, what was this brigade made of; do you know? I'm not sure you know, but if you do know, could you be a little bit more specific?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Thank you. This was the Jure Francetic Brigade, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Could you tell us why it was called that?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Jure Francetic is an historical figure. He is famous by what he did, and we took him to be the protector of our brigade. We took his name because he's an historical person for the Croatian people.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Historical figure from when, approximately; could you tell us that?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: I see. You talked about the refugees who came to Zenica; there were many of them coming to that city. Do you have an idea of how many refugees came to Zenica to seek refuge?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know the exact number, but I heard on the radio one evening that they were expecting refugees to come from all parts of Bosnia that were under the occupation of the aggressor, and that they were expecting about 50.000 refugees to arrive in the town of Zenica, but I don't know at that time exactly how many refugees there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: If I'm not mistaken -- if I am mistaken, please help me -- but if I'm not mistaken, you said that you had talked with some of the refugees in Zenica, and you also told us that some of these refugees had explained what their situation was, what position they were in. What else could you tell us about that?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I didn't talk much. The refugees that I would meet -- I don't know which period you are referring to -- well, the people from Busovaca, before the conflict broke out in Busovaca, I didn't talk to them really, I only asked them where they were from, but I talked with refugees before that who would come from Potkozarje who would ask for aid in food or clothing. That's as much as I would talk with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: In Zenica, did you ever meet Muslim refugees who told you they had been expelled from Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Muslim refugees? Yes. They were not expelled, no. I did not say that. This is what I said, that I saw women and children who were coming out of a truck that was covered with tarpaulin, and I asked them, "Where are you from?" And they said, "From Busovaca." I thought that they were refugees perhaps from Gorazde, Potkozarje, or wherever they were coming from at the time. That's what I thought. I thought that they were refugees. But I saw women and children. I just thought ...

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: But the people you met were Muslim women and children, and you were told they were coming from Busovaca; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, women and children who were coming from Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Without using the word "expelled" then, have you ever learned for what reason these people who were living in Busovaca had become refugees?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I said that I was surprised when I had heard that they were from Busovaca because I didn't know the reason why they were here. The conflict, meaning the attack on Busovaca, came later, and I don't know how I can -- how free I can be to say, but these civilians were their people. These people had moved their families. Perhaps they had known that there would be an attack on Busovaca so that perhaps they moved their families away.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Could you be a little more specific maybe? According to you, who took that decision, to transfer some families to Zenica?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: This is just an assumption that I am making because the conflict broke out later, the BH army attacked the region of Busovaca, so it's an assumption that I am making that women and children were taken out of Busovaca before the attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: If I understand you well, you assumed or you are assuming that the Muslims themselves decided to make refugees out of the members of their family in order to protect them; they decided to send them away?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I think that members of the BH army or the husbands of those families moved their women and children out to a safe area, to Zenica, because they had known that they will attack Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: So I did understand you well. You also told us about the persecution of which Croatian people in Zenica were victims at the end of 1992 and at the beginning of 1993. I listened carefully to what you were saying yesterday, but I would like to know if you received any information about what happened between January 20th and January 27th in Merdani, in Kacuni, in Strane and in Ocenici?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: On the 25th and on the 26th --

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Between the 20th and the 27th of January.

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: January?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Yes, January of 1993.

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Tell me the exact area, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: In Merdani, in Kacuni, in Strane, in Ocenici?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. No, I did not know what was going on there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: So you never heard anybody say that at that time in these villages the Muslim civilians were arrested en masse and sent to Kaonik prison?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I did not know that. I only new about it a bit later, perhaps in February, that the BH army, on the 26th, attacked Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Do you know what life was like for Muslim civilians living in Busovaca at the time?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know what situation they lived in because I lived in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: You never heard journalists say, for example, or a TV channel say, or a radio broadcast say, or a soldier say, you never heard anybody say anything about what life was like for Muslim civilians in Busovaca, you never heard anybody say anything about whether they were free to move around, for example, were they able to exercise their job freely? Do you know if they were protected physically from any threat?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I shall say now that in January 1992 I worked in the hospital, I was doing my own job, and I realised that something was going on in Busovaca. Sadzida Kubat, my engineer, told me this. She kept provoking me all the time, by the way. She was the person who kept asking me to come into her office, and I heard about it from her. Obviously, she was very well-informed, and I heard from her that people did not have freedom of movement or whatever, but I didn't know that. I heard about it from her, and I had the feeling that she was provoking me a great deal because I was a Croat and she had already heard something about that. I didn't hear about it from anyone else but from her.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this stage, I would like to, if you allow me to do so, I would like to refer the witness to a report that was written by Mr. McLeod, who was an investigator for the ECMM. Mr. McLeod, on May 9th, 1993, met the imam of Busovaca. This investigator, who worked for the ECMM, later on wrote a report dated May 17th, 1993. In that report, he gives detailed information about all the meetings he had, and he gives a lot of details about everything that went on in Vitez and Busovaca, among other towns, in 1993. At this stage, I would like to refer to one of these reports. I think it is a reasonable thing for me to ask that some of these reports be admitted in evidence. One copy of these reports has been handed over to the Defence counsel, of course, but I would like to use part of one of these reports as part of my cross-examination. Would you allow me to refer to these documents?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Terrier, when did you give these documents to the Defence counsel?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: At the beginning of the hearing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Five minutes before it began, I think. This is what Mrs. Slokovic-Glumac is saying. Did you give them all of these reports?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Yes, all of these reports. But I am only going to use a page and a half of a particular report. Can I do so?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Our ruling is a majority ruling, and the Presiding Judge dissenting. We have decided that you are not entitled to produce in court this document because this might jeopardise the rights of the Defence since you have not provided this report in advance to the Defence, at least giving them the opportunity to closely examine that document. However, you might call Mr. McLeod, he is the author of this report, in rebuttal. If you feel that this is important evidence, an important piece of evidence, you could call him as a rebuttal witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I will then go on to another series of questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Let's go on to what happened on April 15th, 1993, Madam. On that particular day, Commander Zivko Totic was abducted, and you also told us that you had seen the place where this abduction had taken place on that very morning, on the morning of the 15th; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: On the 15th of April in the morning, I was at the very site.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Do you know if an inquiry was launched, the aim of which was to know who had abducted Commander Totic, in order to know in what circumstances it had taken place and, of course, this inquiry also aimed to know why the five people who escorted Commander Totic had been killed?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I cannot know whether an investigation took place or not. I can only know what I saw for myself as I passed there. The crime investigation service of the civilian police force of Zenica was there, and no one was allowed to pass that way, and I can only tell you what I saw there. I don't know what happened afterwards, but when I went back to headquarters and during the following three days, 15th, 16th, and 17th, we only received information at headquarters that they are negotiating for the unconditional release of Zivko Totic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: So you went to the HVO headquarters in Zenica and you spent most of the day of the 15th, of the 16th and of the 17th of April there; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Most of the 15th I spent in Cajdras. I was driving around in an ambulance, 16th and the 17th, yes, and the morning of the 18th.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Could you please tell us how the HVO reacted on April the 15th, on April 16th, and on the following dates? What was the HVO's reaction to Commander Totic's abduction?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Chaos prevailed at headquarters. No one talked about anything else. His youngest brother was there. He kept crying and he was walking about nervously. We tried to calm him down. We tried to pacify him, but everybody else was upset too. That was the only thing that people were talking about. They were asking why this happened, how it happened. They were asking for his release. It was chaos. Chaos prevailed. People could not be peaceful. They could not talk calmly and normally. They were just moving around. It was like an ant hill. Chaos prevailed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Were any measures taken by the HVO in Zenica in order to find out what had happened, how it had happened, to find out where Commander Totic had been taken to? Were any measures taken in order to free him or to find him?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I can only say what I heard at headquarters from the brother of Zivko Totic. He asked for the unconditional release of his brother. He kept asking, "What have you done? When is my brother going to arrive?" And they said that they were on the telephone and that they would attend some kind of conference or whatever. But I don't know whether they actually did go or whether they did actually talk about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: On April 15th, did you look at any television broadcast?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: During that same day, on the 15th of April, 1993, you were in the HVO's headquarters in Zenica. Being there, did you gather any information on what the intentions of the BiH Army were?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. No. I did not watch television. I was busy. I was in a particular room at headquarters all the time, and I tried to pacify the people who were there. That was my task there. I gave some people tranquillisers, other people I gave water and lemon, it's not important, but I did not watch television. Those three days I absolutely did not watch television.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: You took care of people who were very tired. They were not physically injured, they were in a nervous state, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Do you remember at all what happened during the night of the 15th to the 16th of April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: 15th to the 16th, I remember nothing. I think that we were wondering about when the funeral of the people who were killed would take place. I cannot recall whether the funeral of my cousin and the other persons who were killed was on the 16th or the 17th. I cannot give an exact answer to that. I think it was the 17th. I think the funeral was on the 17th, but I really don't know anymore. On the evening of the 15th, I left headquarters, I went home to freshen up, and I came back already at 7.30 in the evening. I came back to headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: According to what you remember, was April 16th similar to April 15th, in the sense that chaos reigned everywhere?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: That I do not know. I didn't go anywhere. I spent all the time at headquarters and my home was nearby. I would go home, freshen up a bit, and I would go back. I did not move around town. From the 15th onwards I did not go from there to the town of Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: I understand, but at headquarters what was the atmosphere like? Was the atmosphere a bit calmer or was it still a very electrical atmosphere?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The same. Chaos prevailed. Nothing changed until the 18th. This chaos continued. Very few people were coming in. Most of us who were there at headquarters simply stayed there. So I didn't really hear anything new. Already from the 15th onwards movement was made impossible.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown Prosecution Exhibit 334. Exhibit number 334.

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I can hardly see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Are you able to read the name of the person who signed this document, Madam?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Operative on duty of the Jure Francetic Brigade, Branislav Bosnijak.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Did you know that man?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I met that person only when I fled from Zenica to Busovaca through this humanitarian organisation. I did not know him before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Would you agree with me to say that this report was written by the officer on duty of the Jure Francetic Brigade on April 16th, 1993 at 6.00 in the morning? Would you agree with me to say that this report indicates that the man who signed it was quite happy with the situation which prevailed and, above all, a very calm man? There is no sign of nervousness, which doesn't lead us to think that, as you said, chaos prevailed at the time.

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I described the situation on the date of the 15th, and I said that after that I did not move towards town, but other men were not coming to headquarters, so I thought that the situation was the same as it was on the 15th. Since you are aware of this, I should like to mention that from '92, perhaps until the end of the war, there was a curfew in Zenica, and what it says here is that unarmed civilians could pass and we knew at what time that was. But from the 15th onwards I did not move from that place. And then people from other parts of Zenica were not coming to headquarters, that is to say from Cajdras, Radakovo, Crkvica. The people who were coming into headquarters until then, or who had work to do at headquarters, that is to say people who were staying there from the 15th onwards, practically spent all their time at headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: I understand, but allow me to put the question to you again. When you read this report, don't you agree that contrary to what you said, on April 16th, 1993 at 6 a.m. in Zenica the HVO was fully in control of what was happening, it was fully effective, and the officer on duty, in spite of what had happened on April 15th, was very happy with the situation which prevailed, was quite confident with what was happening?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I think that this document shows that there was no excessive behaviour any more, since these murders had already been committed, as well as the abduction. There weren't any attacks or abductions or any mistreatments as of the 15th. I think that that is what this pertains to. We did not have people visiting headquarters or that part of town from the BiH Army or the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: A moment ago, while answering a question put to you by Mr. Radovic, in relation to the events which took place in Ahmici, you said, if I am not mistaken, that you had never heard anything about these events at the time, that is. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Could you please clarify your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: I'll put the question to you again, Madam. In April, 1993, were you at all informed about what had happened on April 16th, 1993 in Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: In April, on the 16th, '93, no. I did not know what happened in Ahmici. I heard about Ahmici only when I arrived in Busovaca, and that was the end of April or, rather, the beginning of May, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: When was it? Who was it? How was it that you came to learn about what had happened in Ahmici at the end of April or at the beginning of May, 1993?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. At that time I was already a refugee from Zenica. I arrived there and everybody was talking about Ahmici, my own people, the Croats whom I had cooperated with, my co-workers, as well as the people that I was staying with at a Croat home. Before that, in the period between the 16th and the 27th, I had not heard of Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Could you please explain why all these people that you met in Busovaca, and I am in particular thinking of the Croats, why then they were talking so much about Ahmici? What was it about Ahmici that made it such a considerable event in their eyes?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: It certainly wasn't a significant event. We heard about the crime that was committed there, and people were talking about it nonstop.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Madam, please try to help us. Why couldn't you stop talking about it?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Please, I arrived in Busovaca. Before that I had not heard about these events. People were saying that it was bad there, that people were killed there. These were people that I had talked to or, rather, the people I had talked to condemned this. That I know. I know that many civilians were killed there and that is what people talked about.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Yesterday you told us that on April 18th you had been arrested. You were taken into custody until April 20th. According to the documents submitted by Mr. Susak, it seems that you were arrested legally, that is at least what seems to have taken place. Do you agree? Was it a legal arrest which took place?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I did not understand what you said. What is this seeming legitimacy that you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: We have seen a document, a document which refers to a certain number of laws, and a document which is signed by a representative of a particular authority. You have told us at length about these two days you spent in custody. Why? What was your aim? Did you want to complain about the conditions you had to live in or were you aiming to complain about the authority which arrested you? Why did you talk at length about it?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Those two days were crucial days in my life, and I don't think I've been very well since then at all. These two days left quite an imprint on my heart and my soul, and I shall never forget those two days for as long as I live. They brought me in from a civilian bus, or, rather, I was with a group of civilians and there were a few soldiers there who came subsequently, from the hills, and they put us altogether into a bus. They took the soldiers to the house of correction and they took the civilians along too. And then they took the civilians home. At the end, when all the men were taken out of the bus, they came to pick me up and they took me to the house of correction. They took me to some kind of entrance, I don't know, I hadn't entered the actual building yet. It was some kind of a reception. They called from this reception desk. I asked why did they bring me in; is there a warden, a director, whoever there. "I want to ask him why I am there." They took me away. It was 11.30 p.m. when we saw the warden of the prison in the park of the house of correction. I asked him, very kindly, to explain to me why I was there. He said that he didn't know. He was making fun of me. Then I told him to take me to someone who knew, because I knew of my rights. I studied this in secondary school. I realised that according to the Geneva Conventions I was not supposed to be taken into custody because I was medical staff, I was a nurse, after all. When they put me in the cell, I did not receive any papers whatsoever. Two days after that, when they released me, they gave me both of those two papers together. What was important for me was to go home to my children. They asked me for these papers. Rather, it was only the gentleman from UNPROFOR who asked me for those two papers, and they gave them to the police in Busovaca. It is only then that I realised what Article 119 or whatever meant on those papers. And that is when I found that out. I didn't know about it before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Were you mistreated during that period you spent in custody?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I wasn't physically mistreated. I was taken for questioning two or three times within those two days, which means on Monday I was there in the morning and in the afternoon. In the afternoon I was there from 6.00 to 9.00. In the morning they also took me away, and then shortly after that I heard that I was to be released.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Madam, do you know that at the same time, from April 16th to the 1st of May, about 50 women and children whose parents, fathers, cousins, uncles had been massacred in Ahmici were put into custody in the Dubravica school, and that was not a legal arrest at all, because there was no legally registered document which was signed to justify their detention?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I repeat again, from the 16th to the 20th, I didn't know what was happening around me, not even in my own town, never mind outside of it. When I left the house of correction, even then I didn't hear anything that was going on around me. It was important to me just to leave Zenica, and I believed the people, that they would send somebody to collect me. And they said, "Be patient. Don't worry, we will send UNPROFOR to fetch you." So until then I didn't have any idea what was going on. I was out of my mind. I don't even know exactly when I was taken from Zenica to Busovaca. The people who brought me in front of the police station in Busovaca knew that I had no idea what was going on. I even left my bag there where all my documents were. I really was out of my mind. I was only thinking about myself and nobody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Is it for this particular reason also that yesterday you did not mention the shelling of Zenica which took place on April 19th, 1993? I think this is a considerable and significant event, don't you?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I was in the house of correction, and I heard -- whether this was shelling or -- I heard shooting, explosions. I was afraid for my life at that time also. In the house of correction, they also played the news for us, and we knew that there was shooting in the town of Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: You were afraid for your life, Madam, but all the victims were Muslims. There were about 15 dead people, there were about 30 injured people. This is what took place on April 19th, 1993, in Zenica. Do you know that the inquiry showed that the shelling came from the Vitez area? Do you know that these shells had been sent by a rocket launcher belonging to the HVO?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I didn't know about that. I know nothing about that. I only know that in that place, I heard that not only Muslims were killed there, there were others too.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam. I have no further questions for the witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Terrier. Counsel Susak?

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: You mentioned Cajdras a little earlier on. This is where the headquarters were, and there were a lot of civilians there as well. I am thinking about the 18th of April, 1993.

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The 18th of April, 1993, after the withdrawal from Trokuce, we went towards Podbrezje, towards Calici, we arrived in Zmajevac, and then we arrived in Cajdras. All people who were in the command arrived there, so the army, members who were in the command as well the civilians from those settlements that we passed through, they went with us, but many people in the village had heard shooting and they didn't know what was going on. They hid in the cellars of their homes. And then they were used as human shields for the Mujahedin later. They were tied, those people who didn't follow the army, who remained in the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Do you know that a group of civilians went towards Kuber or at the foot of the Kuber towards Vitez?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: You told the Prosecutor just now that as a nurse, you were providing treatment in the health clinic to people who had nervous problems, so we took that you were a psychiatrist. So as a nurse, you were actually giving medical assistance in cases where people were physically injured?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I am not a psychiatrist, but I had some Apaurine drugs in my pocket so people who were under stress, who were nervous because of what was happening, I was offering those tranquillisers so that they would calm down.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Did you provide medical treatment as well? Were there any injured?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Of course, yes. This was my job. So from Podbrezje in the morning, I said they brought the first dead man to me. Then I had Marko Dujak who was wounded and we carried him all the way from the command, so maybe about 800 metres or one kilometre, we went by car; then we continued on foot through the hills and the forest until we arrived in Zmajevac. Then the wounded person was carried -- transported by car as far as the car could go, to the foot of Zmajevac, to the village of Grm, and then from there, they transported him to Cajdras. How, I don't know. I found all this out later. He was wounded. He was shot through the lung. When I arrived to Cajdras, there were five less seriously wounded persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: While you were detained, were you released before anybody else?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I was released in two days. The others remained longer.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Could you please tell us the reasons, the real reasons, for this? Why were you released before everyone else, if you know this, of course?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I think -- because when I left the house of correction, I was visited by Father Bozo Marketic from Cajdras. He asked me whether I was physically abused and also to talk with me. I said I wasn't mistreated physically. I asked whether they were making some kind of recommendation that I be released because I was the only woman who had been detained. He had said, "No," they wanted to have everybody released unconditionally. The woman who was with me in the cell told me that the International Red Cross was supposed to tour the house of correction and that they would give me a toothbrush, toothpaste, and so on. I didn't wait for this because I was released before. I concluded later that I was released because they didn't want the International Red Cross to see me because I was captured and detained while I was still wearing my white uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: You signed your detention order here. I can see your signature on the document. But there is no date. Also, this order on the release, there is no date either. You said that you got both orders only after you left the house of correction.

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. This is correct. I did not receive any kind of document on my arrest. Only half an hour before I was released I was given some papers. They said, "Sign this. You're going home."

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Do you know that when a document is signed in court that the date is more important than the signature?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, I don't know this.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Here, on the detention or the arrest decree, it only says that you have been detained. And then, on the release documents, it says that there are no more reasons for detention. Did anybody explain to you why you were detained?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Did anybody tell you or talk about the facts why you were detained because you answered the question by the Prosecution that you don't know what Article 119 is.

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Nobody explained anything. They kept examining me and questioning me. They kept asking for answers but nobody explained anything because I said at 11.30 p.m., when they brought me to the house of correction, I wanted to meet the warden because I wanted to explain to him that I wasn't supposed to be there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Have you any knowledge about the fact that the region under control of the BH army, they were concealing the illegal arrest and detention of people; do you know this?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: The question is: Did the Muslim authorities conceal the arrest of Croats in the same way as they did in your case by issuing the documents once these people were released, and I'm talking about Croats?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKA TOLIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, if it happened to me, it probably happened to others.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have no further questions, but I ask that these two documents be admitted into evidence, and I have five copies of each one. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document is marked D9/4. The next document is D10/4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: No, because one has already been handed in. It was D8/4. So this one is D9/4.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: D9/4. So there is only one document D9/4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: No, sorry. The one which was already provided to us yesterday is D8/4. So the second one ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Is D9/4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: All right. Since there is no objection from the Prosecution, these two documents are admitted into evidence. There are no questions from the Court. I assume there is no objection to the witness being released. Mrs. Tolic, thank you for testifying in court. You may now be released. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you too. (The witness withdrew)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Could you bring in your next witness, who is not a protected witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: So it is Mrs. Grubesic?

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Mr. Grubesic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Ljuban -- sorry. Mr. Ljuban Grubesic. Yes. Called by yourself, Counsel Slokovic-Glumac, and Counsel Radovic. (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Grubesic. Could you please make the solemn declaration?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: MRS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Good day, Mr. Grubesic. Could you please tell us where you were born, when, and where do you reside and what do you do now?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN GRUBESIC
utterances.text: My name is Ljuban Grubesic. I was born on the 24th of June, 1973, in Kiseljak. I reside in Oseliste. I'm a refugee from Busovaca, and I work in the Busovaca police administration.

utterances.speaker: MRS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: In 1992, you were serving your military term in the JNA?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN GRUBESIC
utterances.text: Yes. I escaped at the end of February '92 from there. I came home and, out of fear that the former JNA would look for me, I left the country. I went to Austria.

utterances.speaker: MRS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Just one moment. When you said you returned home, you returned to Oseliste, the municipality of Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN GRUBESIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MRS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Then you left for Austria?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN GRUBESIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MRS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: And then you returned after some time home to Oseliste?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN GRUBESIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MRS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Where did you begin working when you came back to Oseliste?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN GRUBESIC
utterances.text: Well, I came to Oseliste at the end of October '92.

utterances.speaker: MRS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Where did you start working?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN GRUBESIC
utterances.text: I started to work at the Busovaca police administration at the beginning of November '92.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Well, in order to follow more easily what you will be testifying about, I would like the usher to give you and the Trial Chamber this map.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document is D64/2.

utterances.speaker: MRS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Could you please indicate Oseliste, how many kilometres it is away from Busovaca, and if you could also indicate this on the ELMO, please?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN GRUBESIC
utterances.text: This is Oseliste. It's ten kilometres away from Busovaca. That's this part here (indicating).

utterances.speaker: MRS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Could you indicate Busovaca, please?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN GRUBESIC
utterances.text: (Indicating)

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter can't hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: MRS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: These villages that are next to your village of Oseliste, they are called Gusti Grab, then across the road there is the village of Bukovci, and then some smaller settlements. Are these mainly Croatian settlements in this region between Kacuni and Bilalovac, which are all on the map? If you could indicate Bilalovac on the map, please? Have you found Kacuni; is that right?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN GRUBESIC
utterances.text: (Indicating)

utterances.speaker: MRS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Okay. And Bilalovac?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN GRUBESIC
utterances.text: (Indicating)

utterances.speaker: MRS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: So in this region between Kacuni and Bilalovac on the left side and the right side, are these predominantly Croat settlements at that time? Then Oseliste, where you were born and where you lived, what was the population in Oseliste?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN GRUBESIC
utterances.text: Oseliste was 100 per cent Croat.

utterances.speaker: MRS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: After you started to work in the civilian police, what did you do? Were you an intern, trainee?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN GRUBESIC
utterances.text: Yes. I had the status of trainee, which I fulfilled within six months.

utterances.speaker: MRS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: At that time, in November of '92, was there a joint police in Busovaca? Were both Croats and Muslims members of that police force?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN GRUBESIC
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MRS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: So what happened on the 25th of January of 1993?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN GRUBESIC
utterances.text: On the 25th of January of '93, at about 11.00 a.m., I went to work in Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MRS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: What happened on the way there?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN GRUBESIC
utterances.text: Well, I went down to the road. The bus lines were not operating, so I was hitchhiking. A truck stopped for me, so I took the truck in the direction of Busovaca; and then in Kacuni, close to the mosque, to be more precise, five masked soldiers ran out into the road. They were armed.

utterances.speaker: MRS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Whose soldiers were they?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN GRUBESIC
utterances.text: They were soldiers of the BH army. They were wearing black uniforms and had black caps on their heads.

utterances.speaker: MRS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Then what happened?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN GRUBESIC
utterances.text: When they stopped us, they approached the vehicle with their weapons. They pointed rifles at both of us, on our necks. They told us to come out of the vehicle, and that's what we did. They took my weapons from me, the rifle and the gun.

utterances.speaker: MRS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: You were in uniform?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN GRUBESIC
utterances.text: Yes. So they took the rifle and the gun, they searched us, and then they told us we could go, after which we went into the vehicle again, and we started off in the direction of Busovaca. I arrived in Busovaca, and I reported to my commander what had happened. He called Kacuni, he called the BH army command, and he told them what had happened and asked for these weapons to be returned, if possible. Shortly after that, the phone rang, and my commander answered it, and he was told that there had been shooting in Kacuni, that members of the BH army had attacked the escort of the military police and that there were some injured. This was two people, one of them was a member of the military police, and then afterwards, we found out that the other person was just passing through, he was temporarily there from Konjic.

utterances.speaker: MRS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: So a member of the military police, Ivica Petrovic, was killed then?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN GRUBESIC
utterances.text: Yes. That same day, he was brought to Busovaca, to the health clinic, and that's where I saw him.

utterances.speaker: MRS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: So could you please tell us whether a state of alert was declared, a higher state of alert was declared at that time? Do you have any information about this?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN GRUBESIC
utterances.text: No, I don't know whether the state of alert was declared in the military units.

utterances.speaker: MRS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Was it discovered what had happened in Dusina on that day?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN GRUBESIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MRS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: What happened on the 26th in the morning?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN GRUBESIC
utterances.text: On the 26th in the morning at 6 a.m. the siren went off and it had the general danger tone. And then that day the shooting started around the town and in the town itself.

utterances.speaker: MRS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Who attacked Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN GRUBESIC
utterances.text: Busovaca was attacked by members of the BiH Army.

utterances.speaker: MRS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: So how many days did these combat activities go on for?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN GRUBESIC
utterances.text: The combat went on for about 10 days.

utterances.speaker: MRS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: You were in Busovaca during that whole time?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN GRUBESIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MRS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: You couldn't go home?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN GRUBESIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MRS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: So what did you find out then?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN GRUBESIC
utterances.text: On the 26th of January, 1993, we found out that there was shooting in Dusina, and then on the 27th of January we found out that there were a lot killed in Dusina. We found this out from two of the citizens of Dusina who managed to escape.

utterances.speaker: MRS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: What did you find out about your parents some 10 days after that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN GRUBESIC
utterances.text: Ten days later I was called to the Red Cross and they told me there that both of my parents were killed, and that they had already been buried the day before.

utterances.speaker: MRS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Where were your parents killed?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN GRUBESIC
utterances.text: My parents were killed in our family house in Oseliste, the municipality of Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MRS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: How old were your parents?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN GRUBESIC
utterances.text: My father was 59 years old. My mother was 58 years old.

utterances.speaker: MRS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Where are they buried?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN GRUBESIC
utterances.text: My parents are buried in Badnje, in the municipality of Kiseljak.

utterances.speaker: MRS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: In view of the fact that you didn't see your parents --

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN GRUBESIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MRS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: -- who informed you about where their bodies were found?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN GRUBESIC
utterances.text: After 10 days, from the outbreak of the conflict, the phone lines started to work again, so that my uncle Janko Grubesic called me on the phone and told me what had happened. He saw them. He found out about their murder from Mato Drljepan, who had come to his house and told him that they were killed.

utterances.speaker: MRS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: So could you please tell us whether your father had weapons?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN GRUBESIC
utterances.text: My father never had any weapons.

utterances.speaker: MRS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Was anybody else killed in the village at that time?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN GRUBESIC
utterances.text: Yes, several persons were killed. My parents were killed, as I have stated, Anto Simic was killed, Ante Steko was killed, Niko Kristo, Stipo Pravd and the husband of his mother Kata Pravd.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I suggest we take a break, a 30-minute break.

utterances.speaker: MRS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. We would like to proceed now. So, as regards the death of your parents, you only know about that from the stories of other people, do you?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN GRUBESIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MRS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Tell me, what does your neighbour tell you? Where were your parents killed?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN GRUBESIC
utterances.text: My neighbour, Mato Drljepan, told me that my parents were in his house and that they went back to their own house.

utterances.speaker: MRS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: They were in his house, you said. They actually fled from their own house; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN GRUBESIC
utterances.text: Yes. During the conflict they left their own house and they stayed at his house. After some time they returned to their own home. When the BiH Army came to his house, they told him that they killed Mijo and Anda. He didn't believe it. He headed towards my parents home to check. When he arrived to the house, he saw my father lying dead in front of the house and he ran away. He went in the direction of Kiseljak. Then he came to my uncle's house, my uncle Janko Grubesic, and he told them that my parents had been killed. My uncle got into the car and went to my parents house where he found them dead. My father was lying in front of the house and my mother was in the house. My father was shot in the head and my mother was shot in the back. Somebody had shot through the door. He put their bodies into the house (sic) and went to Kiseljak. They were shooting after him, but he managed to get out. He organised the funeral and they were buried in the village of Badnje, the municipality of Kiseljak.

utterances.speaker: MRS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Mr. Grubesic, could you tell us whether in Oseliste there were any Croats left in that village after the 16th of April?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN GRUBESIC
utterances.text: No, there were no Croats left there.

utterances.speaker: MRS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: In the surrounding villages that you pointed out to us, Gusti Grab, Bukovci?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN GRUBESIC
utterances.text: No, no Croats were left there either.

utterances.speaker: MRS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Tell me, do you know whether the houses were burnt down in those villages?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN GRUBESIC
utterances.text: Yes, I know. Most of the houses were burnt down, almost all of them, and those that were not burned were looted and destroyed. I think that houses were torched up there, according to a certain list. That is what I was told by a neighbour of mine, Mato Drljepan.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Could I please ask the usher to hand out these death certificates.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document D65/2.

utterances.speaker: MRS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Is this the death certificate of your parents?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN GRUBESIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MRS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: And whose else?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN GRUBESIC
utterances.text: This is the death certificate of my parents, of Niko Kristo, Ante Steko.

utterances.speaker: MRS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: So all of them were killed at that time, were they?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN GRUBESIC
utterances.text: Yes, all of them were killed approximately during those 10 days of conflict in the territory of the municipality of Busovaca. And they were civilians.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Could I please ask the usher to hand out these photographs as well.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document D66/2.

utterances.speaker: MRS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Please tell us, Mr. Grubesic, do you know what this is?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN GRUBESIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MRS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Which houses are these? You don't have to look at the list, because it's all there. Are these pictures of houses from your village?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN GRUBESIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MRS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Could you please have a look at this entire file of photographs. Are these houses in Oseliste?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN GRUBESIC
utterances.text: Yes, all of them are in Oseliste.

utterances.speaker: MRS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Tell me, was your house burnt down?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN GRUBESIC
utterances.text: My house was not burnt down, but it was looted completely, so only the bare walls are there.

utterances.speaker: MRS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Tell me, do you know how many houses were burnt down?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN GRUBESIC
utterances.text: I think that from Kacuni to Brestovsko there were over 100 burnt houses.

utterances.speaker: MRS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Were all of them torched at that time, between the 25th of January, 1993 to the 30th of January, 1993?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN GRUBESIC
utterances.text: No, not all the houses were torched in that period of time, only some of them were. The rest were torched after the 30th of January.

utterances.speaker: MRS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Could you also tell us who made this file of photographs?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN GRUBESIC
utterances.text: This file of photographs was made by a co-worker of mine, otherwise a criminology technician at the police office in Busovaca. It was made after the cease-fire was signed.

utterances.speaker: MRS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: All right. One more thing. The map that I first showed you, could we please have a look at that map. This neighbouring village of Gusti Grab, you also said that this is a Croatian village, and Bukovci, across the road?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN GRUBESIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MRS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Could you also show Nezirovici on this map, please. Could you show Dusina and Lasva. In the middle. Yes, you've shown it to us. Could you please show Lasva too. You have to show it here on the ELMO. Very well. Thank you. Please, could you have a look at these other photo files.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document D67/2.

utterances.speaker: MRS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Tell me, can you recognise these houses?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN GRUBESIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MRS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: And from which villages are these houses?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN GRUBESIC
utterances.text: These houses are from the villages of Gusti Grab, Bukovci, and a number of houses are from Oseliste.

utterances.speaker: MRS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Tell me, was this photo file made by your colleague too?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN GRUBESIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MRS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: I would like this photo file to be handed out too, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document D68/2.

utterances.speaker: MRS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Tell me, now we are talking about this photo file. Which villages are these houses from?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN GRUBESIC
utterances.text: In these photo files we can see photographs from the village of Nezirovici.

utterances.speaker: MRS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Are there some houses from Kacuni there too?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN GRUBESIC
utterances.text: It is difficult to discern them in this photo file, because all of the houses were destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MRS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Tell me, was this photo file also made by your co-worker?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN GRUBESIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MRS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Is he the one who took the photographs of destroyed Croat houses in that area?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN GRUBESIC
utterances.text: Yes. He took the photographs of these houses in the villages of Nezirovici, Gusti Grab, Oseliste and Bukovci, and I think partly in Kacuni too.

utterances.speaker: MRS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: On the map that you looked at a few minutes ago, and this part between Kacuni and Bilalovac, do you know, after the January conflict, whether that area remained throughout the war, whether it remained completely separated throughout the war?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN GRUBESIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, this part from Kacuni to Brestovsko, and that's about 15 kilometres altogether. It was completely cut off, so the Lasva River Valley was cut up into two pieces.

utterances.speaker: MRS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: This part between Kacuni and Bilalovac was held by the BiH Army; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN GRUBESIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Mr. President, we have another video clip. We have filmed these houses too. Since I gave the video cassette to the Prosecutor yesterday, we can only look at the introduction, perhaps, and then if the Prosecutor agrees, it can be admitted into evidence without actually viewing the entire tape. These are houses from that area and the filming was actually done after these photo files had been made, and it was done by a criminology technician.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: We feel that since, in any case, we have been handed all these photographs, it is probably not necessary to view the film, and if you wish and the Prosecutor does not object, the videotape could be admitted into evidence. If it is just, I mean, a videotape showing all these --

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: We have no objection, Your Honour. No objection the videotape being admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The videotape is document number 69/2.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MRS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Mr. Grubesic, what happened after the conflict in January?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN GRUBESIC
utterances.text: After the conflict or, rather, after the cease-fire was signed, on the 15th of April, 1993, I heard that in Kuber, in the municipality of Busovaca, there was a conflict between the members of the BH army and the HVO. On that occasion, two members of the HVO were wounded, namely, Dragan Andrijasevic and Slavko Bijelic.

utterances.speaker: MRS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Do you know where they were from?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN GRUBESIC
utterances.text: Both were from Jelinak, the municipality of Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MRS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Do you know what happened in Kuber after that, on the 16th and the 17th of April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN GRUBESIC
utterances.text: Yes. On the 17th of April, in the morning, I was informed -- in the police, of course -- that a conflict had broken out in Kuber, that the BH army had attacked members of the HVO who were up there and that one member of the HVO was wounded. For assistance, we sent out a group from the ranks of the police, a group of eleven persons.

utterances.speaker: MRS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Were you with them?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN GRUBESIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MRS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Where did you go?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN GRUBESIC
utterances.text: I think there were eleven of us. We went to Jelinak where we were taken over or taken under the wing of a member of the HVO who took us to the hill of Saracevica.

utterances.speaker: MRS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: That was an elevation; is that right?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN GRUBESIC
utterances.text: Yes. We went up there, and we found members of the HVO in the forest in positions because the BH army had pushed them back from their positions. So we joined them there and we took up positions in the forest. Shortly after that, a strong attack took place. It was carried out by members of the BH army, so that these men had to retreat. I stayed and a member of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MRS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: What was his name?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN GRUBESIC
utterances.text: Anto Plavcic. So we stayed there for some time, and then after that, Anto Plavcic was killed. After he died, I tried to retreat back towards Jelinak, and I was wounded in my right hand and also I was shot through the lungs. When I was hit in the hand, my right hand was completely shattered. I was bleeding a lot, but I managed to cover about 300 metres. Because I had lost a lot of blood, I fell there and I couldn't get up anymore.

utterances.speaker: MRS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: And then you were captured; is that right?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN GRUBESIC
utterances.text: Yes. After about 15 minutes, a group arrived, a group of members of the BH army, it came from the rear, and it found me there.

utterances.speaker: MRS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: So who rescued you?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN GRUBESIC
utterances.text: A majority wanted to have me killed right there, but one of the group approached, I think he was the commander, he bandaged me and charged four soldiers to carry me to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MRS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: So they took you to the hospital in Zenica; is that right?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN GRUBESIC
utterances.text: Yes. They took me to Zenica, to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MRS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: And you had surgery there?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN GRUBESIC
utterances.text: Yes. After four hours, they brought me in front of the hospital, and that's where I lost consciousness because I had been bleeding for a while, had lost a lot of blood. I don't know after how long, I woke up, and I was in the hospital room.

utterances.speaker: MRS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: What happened in the hospital? Could you please tell us what was the attitude towards you, the attitude of the medical personnel and the soldiers? Did they take care of you?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN GRUBESIC
utterances.text: I wasn't guarded by soldiers. The hospital staff conducted itself correctly, but I was exposed to abuse by the soldiers who would come with weapons, and they threatened that they would kill me. Also, I was very afraid because of the Mujahedin; and when I say "Mujahedin," I mean the foreign nationals who were fighting in the ranks of the BH army.

utterances.speaker: MRS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: When did you leave the hospital and how?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN GRUBESIC
