utterances.text: After 13 days spent in the hospital, I received information that they wanted to take me to the house of correction. I decided to escape from the hospital, which is what I did with the help of people, and I request, for the security of those persons --

utterances.speaker: MRS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: There's no need. You don't need to tell us their names. Where did you hide after that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN GRUBESIC
utterances.text: After I escaped from the hospital, I was hiding for five days in Zenica. I tried, with the help of some people, to get out of Zenica, with the help of UNPROFOR, but they refused.

utterances.speaker: MRS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Were you healed by then?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN GRUBESIC
utterances.text: No. During those five days, I wasn't even bandaged, so I was afraid that my wounds would get infected because they hadn't healed properly.

utterances.speaker: MRS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: So how did you get out?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN GRUBESIC
utterances.text: When I was in Zenica, I received false identity papers in another name, and that's how I managed to transfer to Kakanj. I was there for 17 days.

utterances.speaker: MRS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: And then after that, you go on to Fojnica?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN GRUBESIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MRS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: And then to Kiseljak; is that right?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN GRUBESIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MRS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: So how long did it take to go from Zenica to Kiseljak?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN GRUBESIC
utterances.text: I think it took about 30 days.

utterances.speaker: MRS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: How long did you receive medical treatment after that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN GRUBESIC
utterances.text: For another six months.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Would the usher please give these documents to the Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Counsel Slokovic-Glumac, we were wondering whether we need all these details.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: I am almost finished. I am finished, Mr. President. I just wanted for it to be seen that this story is true. We have confirmed this story, we have corroborated it with documents. I have no further questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document D70/2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Counsel Radovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no questions, but I will probably redirect after the Prosecution, if the Prosecutor intends to use the documents that he gave us today to examine the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: I would also tender documents D64/2 to D70/2 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: No objection? No objection. There is no objection from the Prosecution, so they are admitted into evidence. Mr. Smith?

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Mr. Grubesic, I appear on behalf of the Prosecution team with Mr. Terrier and Mr. Blaxill, and it is my job to ask you a few questions about the information that you have given to the Court today to clarify a few issues. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN GRUBESIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would ask that the witness be shown a map, a map of the area of Busovaca and Kiseljak. My friend, Ms. Glumac, used a map earlier, but this covers a broader area, which would help facilitate the cross-examination. Unfortunately, it's not in colour.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 347.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Mr. Grubesic, do you see the black and white map that I have just placed on the ELMO in front of you to your left?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN GRUBESIC
utterances.text: Yes, I see the map, but I can't read anything on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Perhaps if the map on the ELMO could be placed in front of him? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Mr. Grubesic, this map is slightly more difficult to read, but I have highlighted some of the villages that are around the area that you lived in and obviously around the Busovaca area. Take your time to orientate yourself on the map.

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN GRUBESIC
utterances.text: Yes. It's better now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: The map has highlighted the village of Oseliste; do you see that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN GRUBESIC
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: You mentioned some houses were destroyed in Bukovci, which is just across the road, the main road between Busovaca and Kiseljak? You see Bukovci?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN GRUBESIC
utterances.text: Yes, I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: The other two villages that you mentioned had some destroyed houses further up the road towards Busovaca, Nezirovici and Gusti Grab; you referred to them in your testimony earlier?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN GRUBESIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I said -- but not some houses were destroyed but a large majority of them, practically all of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: You also mentioned, when the photographs were shown to you, that some of the houses in those photograph albums you believed came from -- the photos were from Kacuni.

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN GRUBESIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: But you're not sure which ones they are. Do you know which houses in the photograph albums relate to Kacuni?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN GRUBESIC
utterances.text: I think, if I looked at the captions or the index, then I could indicate a large number of houses from Kacuni, and here I see the house of Andtelko Kvesic which is in Kacuni.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: You stated to the Court that you believed these houses were damaged between the 25th of January and within a ten-day period after that; is that right?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN GRUBESIC
utterances.text: Yes, some were destroyed from the 25th, but I don't know how long this destruction went on. I think for ten or fifteen days after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: You've been told this information from other people; is that right?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN GRUBESIC
utterances.text: Yes, I received this information from other people, but after the cease-fire was signed, I passed through that area and I saw all those destroyed homes -- not all of them, but most of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: The cease-fire was signed on what date; do you remember?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN GRUBESIC
utterances.text: I don't know the exact date.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Was it sometime in February '93?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN GRUBESIC
utterances.text: Yes, I think it was February, ten days after the 25th.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned that -- I think you stated on the 25th of January, you were stopped at a checkpoint at Kacuni by some people you believed to be in the Bosnian army; is that right?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN GRUBESIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was stopped roughly; guns were pointed at my neck.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: You stated that you attended back at the police station in Busovaca. Was it the police commander that rang or was it a military commander that rang the headquarters at Kacuni to find out what was going on?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN GRUBESIC
utterances.text: I didn't say that I returned to Busovaca but that I continued on to Busovaca, and I reported to my commander, the commander of the civilian police, and he called Kacuni, the command of the BH army, but I don't know who he spoke with.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: When did you receive information that someone had been injured at the checkpoint? Was it the same day, the 25th?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN GRUBESIC
utterances.text: Yes, in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: As far as you're concerned, that was when the conflict started, on the 25th, in Kacuni at least?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN GRUBESIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, yes. In Kacuni, near the mosque in Kacuni, to be more precise. As far as I heard, a military police patrol was attacked.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Kacuni is largely a Muslim town; that's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN GRUBESIC
utterances.text: I think that the ratio of the population in Kacuni is about 50-50 per cent, but there are villages, several villages, where there is a Muslim majority.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: In any event, prior to the 25th of January, there was no blockade between Busovaca and Kiseljak; you could gain access from both towns, you could get to work every day?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN GRUBESIC
utterances.text: Yes. I came to work normally, and until then, I had never had any problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: After this ten days of conflict, Busovaca and Kiseljak were separated; you couldn't gain access from one town to the other. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN GRUBESIC
utterances.text: No, you couldn't get to Kiseljak from Busovaca nor from Kiseljak to Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Is it the case that -- tell me if you don't know -- but is it the case that it was from Bilalovac to Kacuni that no access could be gained by HVO soldiers after the ten days of conflict?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN GRUBESIC
utterances.text: No. The BH army would not permit passage.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: That's correct. So in relation to Oseliste and Bukovci, that was a frontline, that area was being fought over between the HVO and the Bosnian army over that ten-day period? If you don't know, just say "I don't know."

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN GRUBESIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, the line, the separation line was in Kacuni and civilians were up there, Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Do you agree with me that in that area that was being fought over by the two armies, over that ten-day period?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN GRUBESIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, there wasn't any fighting up there, and this entire area was under the control of the BH army.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: For that ten-day period, from Bilalovac to Kacuni, there was no fighting in that area; is that what you are saying?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN GRUBESIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: I want to show you a document. It's an order from the commander of the Ban Jelacic Brigade, which is based in Kiseljak. I would like you to read that order and see whether that refreshes your memory about what was happening between Kacuni and Bilalovac over that ten-day period.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 348.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Have you had a chance to read the document?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN GRUBESIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have read the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: You can see it's dated the 27th of January, 1993. In the third paragraph, the last sentence it states, "The Bukovci village must be taken by nightfall on condition that we burn anything standing in our way." Do you see that sentence?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN GRUBESIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: That would seem to indicate that there may well have been fighting between Kacuni and Bilalovac over that ten-day period; does it not?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN GRUBESIC
utterances.text: Since I am not a military man, I find this order a bit strange. I did not have the opportunity to see such documents. And these villages here, the ones mentioned here, are in the territory of the municipality of Kiseljak, so I don't know what was going on up there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Bukovci is in Busovaca municipality; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN GRUBESIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: That's what this order refers to. I think you said in your evidence earlier that Bukovci was a predominantly Croat village. Are you sure about that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN GRUBESIC
utterances.text: No, I did not say that. The majority population was Muslim, but there were about 15 to 20 Croat houses there too.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: You said that the attack on Busovaca by the Bosnian army occurred on the 26th of January. Are you sure that the fighting occurred on the 26th or could you be mistaken about the dates? Could it have occurred on the 25th of January?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN GRUBESIC
utterances.text: I said that on the 25th there was an incident in Kacuni, and on that occasion two persons were killed. They were both Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Did you say that two people were killed or two people were injured?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN GRUBESIC
utterances.text: Killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: What were you doing on the 16th -- sorry, on the 26th of January?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN GRUBESIC
utterances.text: On the 26th of January I was at the police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Within the township of Busovaca on the day that you say the attack occurred, a large number of Muslims were arrested and taken to Kaonik Camp. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN GRUBESIC
utterances.text: I heard about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Are you aware that on the 26th of January, in Loncari, a large number of Muslims from that village were taken to Kaonik Camp?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN GRUBESIC
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Are you aware of a large number of Muslims from the Jelinak village being taken to Kaonik Camp on the 26th of January?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN GRUBESIC
utterances.text: I don't know about that either.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Do you know about Kaonik Camp and what was happening there in January, early February, from the 25th of January to the 10th of February? Do you know what was happening at that place?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN GRUBESIC
utterances.text: I heard that there was a prison over there, but I don't know what was happening there. And I didn't visit that prison either at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Are you aware of a group of about 15 Muslims being taken to the village of Merdani and used as hostages in order that the residents from the village surrender their weapons, the Muslim residents in late January, 1993?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN GRUBESIC
utterances.text: I don't know about that either.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: There's a few more of these situations that I need to put to you, but you seem to be aware of some matters, and I just want to see whether or not you are aware of other events going on in a particular area at the time. There was a group of 15 men taken from Kaonik Camp to a village called Stranjani in late January, 1993, and they were used as hostages so that the Muslims from that village would hand over their weapons. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN GRUBESIC
utterances.text: I am not aware of that event. If something had happened, I think it was done by the army, and I was a member of the civilian police.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: These events are common knowledge to some people, so in terms of if you picked it up from common knowledge, that's why I am asking you. In relation to the village of Skradno, the same incident occurred where 15 Muslims were taken to the village as hostages, so that the male villagers would hand over their weapons to the HVO. Were you aware of that, in late January, 1993?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN GRUBESIC
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that either.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Can you explain to the Court your knowledge of the Kaonik Camp, what it was, and what it was used for in late January, 1993 through to June, '93.

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN GRUBESIC
utterances.text: Although I never went there, I cannot give you the right picture.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: You must have some knowledge, bearing in mind you were involved with the military when you went to Kuber. You assisted in a military operation at Kuber when you were injured. You must be aware of what was happening at Kaonik Camp at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Counsel Radovic, objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I give all credit to the Prosecutor, but he cannot tell the witness what he does know, what he doesn't know. The witness says what he knows and what he doesn't know, and no one can make him know what he doesn't know. So he insists on this question and keeps telling the witness that he has to know that, and I think that that is utterly wrong. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. You are right. I think you should not insist because it's clear that the witness does not know about the Kaonik Camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. There is just one last question I would like to ask.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: In relation to the practice of digging trenches, you said that you went to the Kuber range and I think you fought on the frontline for the HVO; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN GRUBESIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I was at Kuber, but I was sent by my commander. And what co-operation he had with the army, that I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Are you aware of the practice of trench-digging in the Busovaca area in January and February and then April in '93?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN GRUBESIC
utterances.text: I am not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: So you are not aware that large numbers of Muslims, civilians, were used to dig trenches in January and in April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN GRUBESIC
utterances.text: I have been saying that I was a member of the civilian police, and if the army did something, I cannot know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: When you arrived back to Busovaca, Oseliste, I think it was in November, 1992 from Austria; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN GRUBESIC
utterances.text: Yes, I came from Austria.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And the HVO had controlled all of the government offices in the township of Busovaca; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN GRUBESIC
utterances.text: I think that is not correct. I think that the Croats and the Muslims were still together.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Together in the sense of the governing authority in Busovaca, together in the sense of the police and in relation to joint military activity in Busovaca township? In all of those areas are you saying that the Muslims and the Croats were together on equal footing when you arrived back?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN GRUBESIC
utterances.text: As far as political decisions and political activities are concerned, they were together. In the police they were together. As regards the organisation of the army, I am not familiar with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I apologise for interrupting you. Do you have still many more questions, because we may take a break now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: I have about 15 minutes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: So let's take a break and then you resume your cross-examination. Fifteen minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Smith, you said you need about 15 more minutes?

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: I'll be less than that, Your Honour, I think you'll be pleased. About five minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Five minutes. Wonderful. We had hoped we may finish with this witness this afternoon, and we can get through tomorrow with the two remaining witnesses, and also because, as you know, we will skip one week. I imagine the witnesses are around so they should not be required to come back in about ten days. Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Mr. Grubesic, a lot of your testimony has been about what people have told you what happened in these villages, in the villages of Oseliste and Bukovci and the villages in that area. Who were you receiving your information from generally at the time, in April 1993? Was it military or was it friends or both?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN GRUBESIC
utterances.text: I mainly received my information from friends, mostly civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: You mentioned that you received some information about some happenings at Kuber. When did you first receive information about any fighting at Kuber in April '93?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN GRUBESIC
utterances.text: I first heard about it on the 15th, that some incidents occurred up there between the members of the HVO and the BH army. I received this information at the police, from my co-workers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: You were working on the 15th of April; is that right?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN GRUBESIC
utterances.text: No. No, I was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: The first you heard of any incidents at Kuber was when you were told on the 15th of April?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN GRUBESIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. On the 15th of April, in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: What day did you go to Kuber yourself?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN GRUBESIC
utterances.text: On the 17th of April, in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: When was the first that you heard that someone was killed at Kuber? On what day was the first day that someone was killed at Kuber, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN GRUBESIC
utterances.text: I think it was on the 17th, to the best of my knowledge, and Anto Plavcic was killed, a member of the HVO who was with me up there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Was it in the morning of the 17th or in the afternoon?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN GRUBESIC
utterances.text: In the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Are you aware that on the 15th of April, in the village of Jelinak, which is near Kuber, that the Muslim males from that village were arrested and taken to Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN GRUBESIC
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: I seek to tender the exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: -- into evidence? No objection from the Defence? No objection. Thank you. They are admitted into evidence. Now, as for the re-examination, Counsel Radovic or Counsel Slokovic-Glumac? No? Counsel Slokovic-Glumac?

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: I thought you would be doing it [to Mr. Radovic].

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Mr. Grubesic, in the area of Busovaca or in the area of the municipality of Vitez, was there a camp there? Did you hear of a camp being there?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN GRUBESIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: What was in Kaonik? The Prosecutor mentioned it. What was in Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN GRUBESIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, the district prison is there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Is that a big prison? Have you ever been there?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN GRUBESIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Could we please have P348?

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Tell me, is any mention made of Nezirovici, Gusti Grab, Oseliste in this document anywhere?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN GRUBESIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: So no mention is made of any one of the Croatian villages that are on the right-hand side when going from Kiseljak to Busovaca, on the right-hand side of the road? I mean -- yes.

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN GRUBESIC
utterances.text: No, no village is mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: This part above the road, was it predominantly Croatian?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN GRUBESIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Is there a village in this part that was Muslim; do you know that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN GRUBESIC
utterances.text: Yes, there is. The village of Bukovci.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Bukovci is on the lower side, on the left-hand side, below the road; is that right?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN GRUBESIC
utterances.text: Viewed from Kiseljak, they are on the left-hand side of the road.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: So Bukovci was on the left-hand side of the road and it had a predominantly Muslim population, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN GRUBESIC
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps there were some 20 Croat houses.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Bukovci is somewhere where the Kiseljak municipality starts; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN GRUBESIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. The village of Bukovci borders on the Kiseljak municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: The order that was issued was issued by the commander of the Ban Jelacic Brigade in Kiseljak; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN GRUBESIC
utterances.text: Yes, as far as I could read it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Did you know in those days what was actually going on? Did you know that in that part, on the left-hand side, that there was any combat action there?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN GRUBESIC
utterances.text: No, I did not learn about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Where was the war being waged between the BH units and the Busovaca municipality? Was this predominantly in town or in these villages in the immediate vicinity of Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN GRUBESIC
utterances.text: Most of the fighting took place at the separation lines, that is to say, in the surrounding villages.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Tell me, in relation to the villages that the Prosecutor asked you about, that is to say, those that are near Kuber, do you know whether Jelinak had a majority Croat population or a majority Muslim population? Jelinak and Putis.

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN GRUBESIC
utterances.text: I think that the Croat population had a majority.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: What about Putis?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN GRUBESIC
utterances.text: In Putis, there was a mixed population.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Do you perhaps know whether any Croats remained in Jelinak and Putis after these events? Are there any Croats in that area? I'm talking about the events of April 1993, when you said that you were there too.

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN GRUBESIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, Croats fled from that area.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Were Croat houses burned in that area around Kuber too?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN GRUBESIC
utterances.text: As far as I managed to find out afterwards, after the cease-fire was signed, all the houses up there were either burned or destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: I have one more question regarding these events. Do you know what happened in Kuber on the 16th? Was there fighting in Kuber then? You said that you had information about a conflict on the 15th, and then you know that on the 17th, there was fighting. Did you participate, and was there any fighting on the 16th?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN GRUBESIC
utterances.text: I think, yes, there were incidents.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Do you know in which part, whether this was from the side of Busovaca or from the Vitez side of Kuber?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN GRUBESIC
utterances.text: From the Busovaca side.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Do you know in which places this happened?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN GRUBESIC
utterances.text: I don't know the terrain up there very well. I only know that the point, elevation where I was, is called Saracevica, and near it there were some incidents.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I have no more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. There are no questions from the Court. Mr. Grubesic, thank you for giving evidence in court. You may now be released. Thank you. (The witness withdrew)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: We move on to Mr. Stojak. Yes, Counsel Susak?

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have a request before we start with the next witness. I would like to ask the Prosecution one question, and I also suggest that we move into closed session because we will now mention some names.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes. (Closed session)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: (Open session) (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojak, good afternoon. Could you please make the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good day, Mr. Stojak.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJAK
utterances.text: Good day.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Could you please tell us where you come from and your date of birth.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJAK
utterances.text: I was born on the 30th of November, 1962 in Vitez, and I am permanently residing in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: What is your occupation?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJAK
utterances.text: I am a professor of All People's Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Are you married? Do you have children?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJAK
utterances.text: Yes, I am married. I have two children.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Could you please tell us where you were employed before the war.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJAK
utterances.text: On the 1st of June, in 1991, I started to work at the intelligence centre in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Where did you work before that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJAK
utterances.text: I wasn't working anywhere. After university I spent two years on temporary work in Switzerland, and then, when I came back from Switzerland, I started to work at the centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: How long did you work there?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJAK
utterances.text: Until the 15th of August, 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Were any Muslims employed in the centre?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJAK
utterances.text: Yes. There were Muslims there. They were employed there permanently.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Could you give us some examples.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJAK
utterances.text: Yes. When I came to the centre for intelligence, when I started to work there, Nedin Zlotrg was my boss. He was the chief, the head of the centre. And then also there were also Rasad Zlotrg, Vladica Babic and myself who were working there. And Dragan Bilatic as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: So how many were employed there?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJAK
utterances.text: There were four operatives working at the centre, and one head of the centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Is this centre -- was it later expanded, as far as the staff was concerned?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJAK
utterances.text: In the course of aggression against Slovenia and Croatia, the staff was increased mainly by volunteers, because there was more work to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Were there any changes in the centre? Was there any reconstruction carried out during the war?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJAK
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: But it more or less remained as it did?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJAK
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: How did you get information? Could you please tell us whether there were any visual observers?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJAK
utterances.text: Yes. We formed visual observers in the neighbouring villages, because our centre, one of its duties, among others, was to alert the population, and with the escalation of the aggression against Croatia and Slovenia, there was a need to place visual observers because we were afraid of air attacks on Vitez. We mainly used people from the neighbouring villages, so the local population, because we couldn't pay them or compensate them in any other way, so they worked on volunteer basis. They were those who would generally give us information, mostly by telephone, and sometimes they would send messengers, depending on the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: So you had this intelligence centre. Were you close to the Crisis Staff, and who was in the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJAK
utterances.text: Before the 16th, before the combat activities began, we were buildings next to each other, so the centre for intelligence was located in the cellar of the post office, and this is what was the situation before and it still is the situation. The Crisis Staff was in the municipal building that was next door. Then at the beginning the Crisis Staff moved close to us. It also went to a separate room in the cellar of the post office.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: So did you have all the information available at the centre or did the Crisis Staff have some information that you didn't have?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJAK
utterances.text: No, we didn't have all the information. We mostly received and distributed mail. However, this mail would often bypass us and would go where it was supposed to directly, so --

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Mr. President, may I just take a second. There is a problem with the translation. We don't want this whole testimony to go in a wrong direction, because it would lose meaning. Mr. Stojak worked in the centre for information. It's not intelligence, intelligence centre. It's a centre to provide information of what is going on so to -- it's like an alarm system in case of need, to alarm the population of what's going on. In war and peace this centre operates. So its purpose is not to gather intelligence, but to provide information about what is going on. So the translation is wrong.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: So now we will be more specific. You said that this centre -- did it also deal with other kind of events, because you said information in case of something. So would you please tell us what this something is?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJAK
utterances.text: Well, I said, amongst other duties -- maybe to clarify to this Trial Chamber. This centre for information, 985, is like the centre 911, the emergency number. It's connected to the hospital. So it's used to convey information to certain institutions, depending on what the situation called for.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: So now I will ask you. You are talking about this centre. You said that nothing had changed. Did the centre carry out the same duties before the war and after the war?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: All right. Because you are closely connected to the defence office, do you know what the purpose of the defence office was?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJAK
utterances.text: Before the war or after the war?

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Before the war and after the war.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJAK
utterances.text: The defence --

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Well, before the conflict and after the conflict.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJAK
utterances.text: The defence office, in the earlier system, usually maintained records of military conscripts, it sent the conscripts to serve their military duty in the then JNA, but with the aggression against Croatia, all of this was suspended, so the office did not carry out these duties anymore. It maintained records, purely the paperwork that is appropriate to such an office, and then new developments occurred. So as part of the --

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Mr. Stojak, would you please speak more slowly because this has to be interpreted?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJAK
utterances.text: The component of that office was us, the centre for information, and then the sector for civilian defence, that was a sector of the civil defence department, and then in the times of war, this service would really take care of the disabled, would help children, it would distribute aid and food to these needy categories of people.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Do you know when mobilisation was carried out in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJAK
utterances.text: Mobilisation in Vitez began on the 16th of April in 1993, sometime in the second part of that day, approximately.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would ask the usher to show the witness a Prosecution document 335.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: If you've had a look at it ... If you had a look at it, Mr. Stojak, we would like to concentrate on this written report first and foremost. What does it mean that the defence department, in addition to its regular work, has also established the Vitez Brigade and a working group has been set up together with other people from the defence department?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJAK
utterances.text: I said a few minutes ago that from earlier on, we had those records, those lists of conscripts. It was only natural, in terms of military hierarchy, that the defence department, together with someone from the brigade headquarters, would call up conscripts in a case of war, immediate threat of war, or other such situations.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Now we're going to see point 3. What does that mean, "from the 16th of April up to and including 28th April, 1993, a total of 498 conscripts were mobilised and actively included in HVO units, in addition to the regular personnel of the Viteska Brigade." First of all, may I remind you of the following: Is it possible for 498 conscripts to be mobilised in a single day?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJAK
utterances.text: I said a few minutes ago that mobilisation started on the 16th of April, sometime during the latter part of the day, that is to say that there was still commotion at this initial stage of the war. Four hundred ninety-eight is a viable figure but only on paper, only in terms of records. People were registered in this war situation. So in terms of paper, this was done, but I don't think in practical terms, 498 conscripts could have actually been mobilised, I mean actually taken to trenches or into battle or whatever, because -- there would be an example of this in these lists. I know quite a few of these people, and if I were to look at these lists very carefully, I could certainly find even more examples, but I know some of these people. Obviously, for example, numbers 85 and 86. It is mentioned here that Vojvodic Miro and Vojvodic Zoran were mobilised. Those are two brothers. But it is well-known that they worked as translators for the U.N. then. Nowadays, it is called IFOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Could they have been mobilised if they worked for UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJAK
utterances.text: Who could have informed them at UNPROFOR and who could have got them out of UNPROFOR? Ordinary people, people from the defence department, et cetera, I mean, who could have gone into the UNPROFOR camp?

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: So nobody had access to the UNPROFOR camp and there was no cooperation in this respect; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJAK
utterances.text: No, no. Only high officers could enter UNPROFOR premises, but this was much later. And also I have the example of Dragan Pavlovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Which number is that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJAK
utterances.text: Just a minute. Just let me have a look at it. Two hundred twenty-six.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: What did you want to say about Pavlovic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJAK
utterances.text: This gentleman was the director of a company in Vitez, and he was away on business in the Republic of Croatia, in Ploca, and he spent the entire war there, so he didn't even show up in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: So how could he have been mobilised?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJAK
utterances.text: Because mobilisation as such means that, first and foremost, all of this has to be done on paper, and then the relevant team goes out and distributes call-up papers to all the persons who are supposed to be mobilised. There are probably other examples of this nature, but we don't have enough time, I imagine, to go into an in-depth analysis right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Could you establish that some person from this list was mobilised after the 16th of April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJAK
utterances.text: Well, probably. Probably most of these men were because the mobilisation started in the latter half of the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: This period is the 16th of April until the 28th of April inclusive; that's what this paper says.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJAK
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: So it's not possible practically to do this in one day?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJAK
utterances.text: No, practically, it is not possible to do this in one day.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Since you have a degree in national defence; is that correct --

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: -- so what does that mean, that most of these conscripts were involved in frontline activities from the very first day?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJAK
utterances.text: Where is this?

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: This is under point 3 on the first page of this report.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJAK
utterances.text: That means that these 498 conscripts were directly involved in HVO units. However, during a military conflict, it is only natural that the people from the Viteska Brigade would take the first attack; and then, as mobilisation proceeded, then they received additional manpower as listed here.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: So you think that these reserve units could not have taken part in the first repulsion or the first attack?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJAK
utterances.text: They couldn't have.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: You also have another sentence down here that the mobilised persons are being used as replacements on the lines after the first assault. How long can this go on, for several days or not? These replacements, I mean.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJAK
utterances.text: Well, at any rate, it is the regular units that take the first attack. However, as ranks are stabilised, then replacements come in, and this can go on until an official document says the mobilisation is over. However, mobilisation could not have been over throughout combat activities because additional personnel were needed all the time and also additional logistics.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Could you please explain what mobilisation means, in your opinion, or can you explain what mobilisation along automatic lines means, or what does it mean in military terminology?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJAK
utterances.text: In military terminology, mobilisation along automatic lines means that there were certain records that, in some office, there were files on individual persons, and as soon as mobilisation is declared, people are taken from these records automatically and a list is being made of the persons who would be considered. Then a list is made of persons who should be mobilised during a certain period of time, not only --

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Please slow down.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJAK
utterances.text: But also all the logistics needed are listed too, that is to say, vehicles, fuel, whatever is necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: In Vitez, there were quite a few Muslims and Serbs and others who were military conscripts. Did this make it increasingly difficult to make up lists and to receive information as to who the military-age men actually were?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJAK
utterances.text: Well, at any rate, this was difficult because there could have been a man who was a Serb, for example, on this list, because at that time, there was pronounced migration. Serbs, for example, moved to some other areas, and very often they would simply leave without saying good-bye or without reporting to anyone. Since these records existed from earlier on, it is only logical that this person could have been in these records and on these lists, and when these things are done automatically, his file could have been found too and his name could have been on the list for mobilisation. However, the man would not even be there in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Were there any Croats from Vitez who waged war in other territories in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJAK
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Were such persons deleted from the files of the defence department of Vitez?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJAK
utterances.text: They were not, more or less, deleted from these records of the defence department. Those who were diligent enough to report to this department simply had it registered there, that they had changed their place of residence or that they were engaged in battle elsewhere. Often this was not the case. They would simply go. They would go to a battlefield of their own free will. Voluntarily, I mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: As far as I could understand what you were saying, you could not have up-to-date records; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Is this perhaps due to the fact that many people who were military-age men were in villages too?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: So that was one of the reasons too; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJAK
utterances.text: Yes. Very often, in these post-war days, people were trying to find jobs and a better living elsewhere, and they went elsewhere, they went to other frontlines voluntarily. But in most cases, they did not realise that they were supposed to report to the police, the defence department, and the municipality, wherever, they would simply leave. That made it more difficult for the persons employed in the defence department. They could not have known where somebody was at a given point in time had somebody not reported to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Now I would like to move on to another question of a similar nature, and that is civil defence. Could you please tell us how it operated and how it was organised before the 16th of April, 1993, and what happened to the civil defence afterwards?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJAK
utterances.text: Civil defence was part of the defence department, it was a segment of the defence department. I said a few minutes ago that it primarily dealt with providing accommodation and care for the needy, for the famished. Very often during the war they also tried to provide accommodation for refugees from other parts of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and they distributed food to these people too, to the extent to which this was necessary. For that purpose, they established some kind of a mini-staff of their own of the civil defence where they had their representatives on the ground; that is to say, in different parts of Vitez, in villages, so that these activities could be carried out as quickly as possible and in the best possible way. So, for example, food was to be distributed in Kruscica. Then they would call their representative there and then they would make arrangements for such and such a date for food to be distributed in front of such and such a person's house according to a list that was provided by one of the representatives of the civil defence. When war operations started or, rather, when the aggression took place in our parts, it became necessary to establish within the civil defence teams of persons for --

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'm going to interrupt you at this point, Mr. Stojak, because I want to put a question to you and to remind you of something. Was any decision reached on the 16th or 17th of April, 1993, by the head of staff of the civilian defence; do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJAK
utterances.text: Yes. In keeping with the orders issued by the head of the staff of civil defence, and I imagine that he had received orders from the head of the crisis staff of the municipality of Vitez, I imagine that he gave him the green light to set up this team for improvements, and I think that this team was established sometime on the 17th of April; that is to say, on the second day of the war, because there were so many persons who were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: You mentioned the head of the crisis staff. Who is this person in the case of the municipality of Vitez?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJAK
utterances.text: At that time, it was the legally elected mayor of the town of Vitez, Mr. Ivan Santic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: So does this office coincide with that of the head of the crisis staff? Is that to say that the mayor and the head of the crisis staff are one and the same person?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJAK
utterances.text: Yes, yes. These two offices coincide. This is also done automatically.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Mr. President, I believe that this would be a good point to adjourn because we have quite a few questions left, and I imagine our time is up. Of course, it is up to the Trial Chamber to rule on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Do you have a rough idea of how much time you still need?

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Less than an hour, around an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Do we know how many Defence counsel intend to cross-examine this witness? Of course, you may react -- you don't know yet. Yes. Because, as I say, we must by all means finish tomorrow with this witness and the other witness as well. Let me, before we adjourn, first of all, remind the Prosecutor that tomorrow he should not only give us some information about the document mentioned before by Counsel Susak but also about the expert witness statements. Also, I would like to let you know about our plans for the timetable for the months of April and May. Since this Trial Chamber will -- or some members of this Trial Chamber will be sitting on other cases, in April we will be sitting on Kupreskic only the last week of April, starting on the 26th, only one week; then in May, the first week of May and last week of May, the week starting on the 3rd up to the 7th and then from the 24th to the 28th, just for your information, because we assume you have to make plans. We have now been told about the planning for other cases, and so I thought it only appropriate to let you know in advance. So we are adjourned now until tomorrow at 9.00 sharp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: 6.05 p.m., to be reconvened on Friday, the 29th day of January, 1999, at 9.00 a.m. 25
